stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set at a rural experiment station. Halloway, a farmer, has asked the station chemist, Pryce, why his wheat yields keep falling.
HALLOWAY: I have manured that field every autumn, as my father did. Surely the fault lies in the seed.
PRYCE: Thou mayst change thy seed a dozen times, and still the yield will fall. That field has borne wheat for three generations, and every harvest carried off what the manure never put back. Sow it with clover two seasons, then come ask me about seed.
choices: Halloway insists that his poor harvests must come from faulty seed, since he has manured the field faithfully.
Pryce contends that changing the seed will raise the yield only if it is done many times over several seasons.
Pryce contends that the falling yields come from years of wheat draining the soil rather than from the seed.
Pryce contends that manure has done the field no good and that wheat should be abandoned there permanently.
explanation: The introduction tells you Pryce is answering Halloway's question, so Pryce's reply carries the point. In plain English: changing the seed won't help, because three generations of wheat have taken out more than the manure put back, so plant clover for a while. Choice C states that claim: the soil is worn out, and the seed isn't the problem.

A.why: You summarised the other character's line. Halloway's view about the seed is the idea Pryce sets out to correct, so it isn't the point the text lands on.

B.why: You read 'a dozen times' literally. Pryce means that no amount of seed-changing will help ('still the yield will fall'). He isn't telling Halloway to do it more often.

D.why: Pryce says the manure 'never put back' everything the harvests took. He doesn't say it did nothing. He also suggests clover for two seasons, which is not the same as giving up wheat for good.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from an imagined dialogue written to defend an early form of vaccination. Lysander, a worried father, questions Theron, a country physician.
LYSANDER: You would have me scratch my daughter's arm with matter from a cow's sore. Is it not madness to give a healthy child a disease?
THERON: And is it wisdom to leave her open to one that kills? The milkmaids of this parish took the cowpox and were well within a week; when smallpox swept through, not one of them sickened. If a mild illness can stand guard against a deadly one, then the madness lies in refusing it.
choices: Theron argues that a mild infection is worth accepting because it appears to shield against a deadly one.
Lysander objects that deliberately giving any disease to a healthy child is an irrational thing to do.
Theron admits that leaving a child unprotected may be wiser than taking the risk of inoculation.
Theron argues that the milkmaids of the parish are naturally immune to every illness that passes through.
explanation: Theron's claim sits in his closing conditional: if a mild illness can protect against a deadly one, then refusing it is the real madness. The milkmaids are his evidence. Choice A restates that argument.

B.why: This summarises Lysander's speech, which is the objection Theron answers. It isn't the point the passage builds toward.

C.why: You took Theron's rhetorical question literally. 'Is it wisdom to leave her open to one that kills?' means it is not wise. He is pushing for inoculation, not conceding.

D.why: Theron says only that the milkmaids didn't catch smallpox after having cowpox. He never says they resist every illness, or that their protection was natural rather than caused by the cowpox.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Two excavators, Corbett and Ines, are examining a buried hearth at a site that published accounts describe as a brief seasonal camp.
CORBETT: A single hearth. Hunters stopped here one autumn, cooked, and moved on. The textbooks say as much.
INES: Then tell me why the clay floor beneath it has been replastered seven times. Travelers passing through don't mend a floor they will never see again. Whoever cooked here came back, year upon year, or never left at all.
choices: Corbett maintains that the hearth shows hunters used the site only briefly, just as published accounts claim.
Ines asks Corbett to explain the replastering because she cannot account for the repairs herself.
Ines argues that the replastering proves the site's occupants had built permanent stone houses nearby.
Ines argues that the repeated replastering shows the site was used over a long period rather than once.
explanation: The introduction sets up the accepted view, and Ines's reply overturns it. The seven layers of plaster point to people who returned or stayed, because short-term visitors don't repair a floor. Choice D captures that challenge.

A.why: This is Corbett's position, the textbook view Ines argues against. Choosing it means you matched the wrong speaker.

B.why: You took 'tell me why' literally. Ines isn't stuck. She is making a point and already gives the answer: the people came back or never left.

C.why: Ines talks only about the replastered floor and repeated use. Nothing in the text mentions stone houses, so this claims more than the evidence supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set at a coastal weather station in the 1870s. Abel, the station keeper, is reassuring his assistant, Ruth, who has been watching the barometer all afternoon.
ABEL: Sky's clear as glass, and the wind's dropped to nothing. We'll have a fine night of it.
RUTH: A fine night, says he, and the glass fallen a full inch since noon. Ere morning that calm will have teeth. When did still air ever hold off a falling barometer? Bring in the boats.
choices: Abel argues that the clear sky and the still wind show that the coming night will be calm.
Ruth warns that the falling barometer signals a coming storm despite the calm conditions.
Ruth wonders whether still air has ever stopped a barometer from continuing to fall.
Ruth warns that the barometer has failed and can no longer be trusted to predict weather.
explanation: Put Ruth's lines into plain English: the barometer has dropped sharply, so the calm will turn violent before morning, and the boats should come in. Choice B states her warning.

A.why: This is Abel's reassurance, which Ruth mocks ('A fine night, says he'). You matched the character who is being corrected.

C.why: Ruth's question is rhetorical. She means calm air has never held off a storm that a falling barometer predicts. She isn't genuinely wondering.

D.why: This reverses Ruth's position. She trusts the barometer and acts on it. It's the clear sky she distrusts.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Three weeks before a championship, Coach Delaney wants his runners training hard every day. The team physiologist, Dr. Osei, responds.
DELANEY: Every day they rest is a day the other teams gain on us.
OSEI: Gain what? A muscle isn't built during the run. It is torn a little, and it rebuilds in the hours afterward. Take those hours away and you are only tearing. If you want them fastest on race day, then the easy days are part of the training, not a holiday from it.
choices: Delaney argues that rest days let rival teams pull ahead of his runners before the final.
Osei argues that hard runs damage muscles and should be dropped in the weeks before a race.
Osei argues that recovery days are essential because muscles strengthen while rebuilding.
Osei argues that muscles grow mainly during runs, so the team should keep training daily.
explanation: Osei's claim sits in his final conditional: if you want the runners fastest, the easy days count as training. His reasoning is that muscle rebuilds after effort, not during it. Choice C states both parts.

A.why: This restates Delaney's worry, which Osei is answering. It's the other character's line, not the point the text makes.

B.why: Osei says hard runs tear muscle a little, but he never says to stop them. He wants them balanced with recovery days. This half-right choice names his topic and then attaches a claim he doesn't make.

D.why: Osei says the opposite: 'A muscle isn't built during the run.' You may have lifted words from the passage without checking what they say.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in a seventeenth-century woodcut workshop. The apprentice Tobias has complained that the master's blocks print faintly; the master, Hendrick, replies.
TOBIAS: The lines come out pale and broken. Cut deeper, master, and the ink will hold.
HENDRICK: Deeper? Cut deeper and thou dost but carve away wood that never touched the paper. 'Tis the raised face that prints, boy, not the hollow. Thy fault lies in thy dabber: ink thinly and evenly, press firm, and the paleness goes.
choices: Tobias proposes that cutting the block more deeply would allow its lines to hold more ink.
Hendrick argues that the block must be recut because its printing surface has worn too smooth.
Hendrick asks whether deeper cuts are wise and leaves that decision to his apprentice.
Hendrick argues that the faint prints come from poor inking, not from how deeply the block is cut.
explanation: In plain English, Hendrick says that cutting deeper only removes wood that never prints, because the raised surface does the printing, and that Tobias's uneven inking is the real problem. Choice D states that diagnosis.

A.why: This is Tobias's suggestion, the one Hendrick rejects. You chose the other character's speech.

B.why: Hendrick never says the block is worn or needs recutting. He blames the apprentice's dabber, meaning how the ink is applied.

C.why: 'Deeper?' is a scornful rhetorical question, not a real one. Hendrick rejects the idea immediately and doesn't hand the decision to Tobias.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. After a month of small tremors, the town's mayor, Fenwick, speaks with a visiting geologist, Dr. Asante.
FENWICK: Forty little shakes, and not one cracked a cup. Surely the ground is letting off its pressure gently, a bit at a time.
ASANTE: I wish it worked so. But a fault that slips by inches has not paid down a debt of yards. Swarms like this have come before large earthquakes about as often as they have simply faded. They may mean nothing, but they are no reason to stop inspecting the school.
choices: Asante argues that the small tremors offer no assurance of safety, so precautions should continue.
Fenwick suggests that the frequent small tremors are harmlessly releasing the fault's pressure.
Asante argues that the small tremors show a large earthquake will certainly strike the town soon.
Asante argues that the small tremors have already released most of the strain stored in the fault.
explanation: Asante's 'But' rejects Fenwick's comforting idea. Small slips don't relieve much of the stored strain, and swarms like this one are as likely to come before a large earthquake as to fade away. Her hedge, 'They may mean nothing,' leads into her real point: keep the precautions going. Choice A fits both her doubt and her caution.

B.why: This is Fenwick's hope, which Asante rejects ('I wish it worked so'). You matched the wrong speaker.

C.why: You ignored Asante's hedge. She says swarms come before large earthquakes about as often as they fade, and that they 'may mean nothing.' That rules out 'certainly.'

D.why: Asante says the opposite: inches of slip haven't 'paid down a debt of yards,' so most of the strain is still there.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set aboard a whaling ship in the 1840s. The cook, Pell, is defending the crew's diet to the ship's surgeon, Haddon.
PELL: Salt pork fills a man's belly, and a full belly never yet went sick. Give them enough of it and they'll want for nothing.
HADDON: Enough of it? They've had their fill every day since we left port, and still their gums bleed. A belly may be full and the body starve all the same. 'Tis not how much they eat but what. Put the limes back on the table.
choices: Pell maintains that a crew given plenty of salt pork will stay healthy throughout a voyage.
Haddon argues that the crew's illness stems from what their diet lacks, not how much they eat.
Haddon argues that the crew has been underfed and needs larger daily portions of salt pork.
Haddon argues that salt pork is itself poisonous and is the direct cause of the bleeding gums.
explanation: Haddon's key sentence is 'Tis not how much they eat but what.' The crew have eaten their fill and are still sick, so something is missing from their food, and the limes should come back. Choice B states that point.

A.why: This summarises Pell's speech, the view Haddon is answering. You picked the other character's claim.

C.why: Haddon says the crew have 'had their fill every day.' Quantity isn't the problem, so more pork isn't his fix.

D.why: Haddon blames what the diet is missing, not anything harmful in the pork. Calling it poisonous claims more than he says.
